prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.

text:
Imagine that Alice and Bob have never met and share no password, yet want to finish a conversation both knowing the same secret number while Eve, who reads every message passing between them, ends up knowing nothing useful. This looks impossible, because anything Alice says to Bob, Eve hears as well, and for most of history secret writing assumed that both sides had agreed a key beforehand by meeting in person or sending a trusted courier. The idea that overturned this assumption was published in 1976 by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, and it rests on an observation about arithmetic: some calculations are quick to carry out but practically impossible to reverse, so a person who holds a private number can use the quick direction while everyone else is left facing the slow one.

A picture with paint makes the structure clear before any numbers appear. Suppose Alice and Bob agree out loud, in front of Eve, on a shared colour such as yellow. Alice privately picks a secret colour of her own, say red, mixes it into the yellow and sends the resulting orange to Bob, while Bob does the same with a secret blue, producing a green that he sends to Alice. Mixing paint is easy but unmixing is not, since nobody looking at a pot of orange can say which exact shades went into it, and so Eve, who has seen the yellow, the orange and the green, cannot recover either secret colour. Now Alice adds her private red to the green she received and Bob adds his private blue to the orange he received, and both pots hold exactly the same brownish mixture of yellow, red and blue, because the order in which paints go in does not change the result, whereas Eve would need a red or a blue she has never held to make the same pot.

To turn this into mathematics we need an operation that behaves like paint, meaning that it is easy to do forwards, hard to undo, and indifferent to the order of the steps. Powers satisfy the last condition, since raising a number to the power a and then raising the result to the power b gives the same answer as doing b first and then a, just as 2 cubed and then squared gives 64, which is also what you get from 2 squared and then cubed. What powers lack is difficulty, because anyone told that 8 is 2 raised to some power can see that the power is 3. The remedy is clock arithmetic, where numbers wrap around after reaching a fixed size, as you already know from telling the time, since five hours after nine o'clock is two o'clock because the twelve is thrown away, and in that spirit mathematicians write "mod 23" to mean that you divide by 23 and keep only the remainder, so that on a clock with 23 positions the number 25 becomes 2 and every answer lands somewhere between 0 and 22.

Here is a complete exchange with small numbers. Alice and Bob publicly agree on the clock size 23 and on the base number 5, and Eve hears both. Alice secretly chooses 6, works out 5 to the power 6, which is 15625, divides by 23 and keeps the remainder, which is 8, and sends Bob the number 8. Bob secretly chooses 15, works out 5 to the power 15 in the same way, obtains a remainder of 19, and sends Alice the number 19. Alice then raises the 19 she received to her own secret power, and 19 to the power 6 leaves a remainder of 2 on the 23-hour clock, while Bob raises the 8 he received to his own power, and 8 to the power 15 also leaves a remainder of 2. Both now hold the number 2, which neither ever transmitted, and the reason is the one from the paint: each has in effect computed 5 raised to the power 6 times 15, one by passing through Alice's 6 first and the other through Bob's 15 first, and the wrap-around does not disturb this because remainders can be taken at any stage without changing the final remainder.

What Eve has seen is the clock size 23, the base 5 and the messages 8 and 19, and to reach the secret 2 she would need one of the private powers, which means finding what power of 5 leaves a remainder of 8. With numbers this small she could simply try 1, 2, 3 and so on until she reached 6, so the example demonstrates the pattern and offers no protection, which comes entirely from scale. In real use the clock has hundreds of digits, or the same idea is carried out on a more elaborate object called an elliptic curve that gives the same one-way behaviour with shorter numbers, and the private powers are equally enormous. Computing a huge power on such a clock is still fast, because you can square repeatedly and combine the pieces, but nobody knows a method for finding the power from the result that is much better than trying possibilities, and there are so many possibilities that all the computers on Earth working for the age of the universe would not get through a meaningful fraction of them. Decades of searching have turned up no general shortcut, although none has been proved impossible, so the security rests on well-tested belief and not on a theorem.

The word "public-key" comes from the way the numbers divide into two kinds, since each person's private number, such as Alice's 6, never leaves her possession while the number derived from it, such as her 8, can be printed in a newspaper without harm. Other systems, such as RSA, rest on a different one-way operation, multiplying two huge prime numbers together, which is easy, against splitting the product back into its primes, which is not, and they let a sender lock a message to a recipient's public number so that only the matching private number opens it. In everyday use, such as when your browser connects to a bank, these methods mainly agree a shared secret as above, which then feeds a fast ordinary cipher that scrambles the traffic, because public-key arithmetic is too slow for large amounts of data.

One weakness remains, which is why real systems have more machinery around them than this account has shown. Eve could intercept the messages and pose as Bob to Alice and as Alice to Bob, agreeing one secret with each and relaying the conversation while reading all of it, so that the arithmetic works perfectly and protects nobody. The defence is for each side to be sure that a public number really belongs to its claimed owner, which trusted organisations arrange by vouching for it with digital signatures, a relative of the same mathematics in which a private number produces a stamp that anyone can check against the public number but nobody can forge without it. Even so, the central trick remains one of the most surprising results in practical mathematics: two strangers can build a shared secret in plain sight, because the hard part, undoing a power on an enormous clock, is left in Eve's hands while the easy part belongs to the people who hold the private numbers.
